messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David remembers the rain. It was a cold, driving rain last October, the kind that streaks the windows and makes the world outside feel distant and gray. He was in the living room, half-watching a financial report on the television, when he heard his wife scream from their son’s nursery. That moment cleaved his life into a before and an after. The image of his two-year-old, impossibly small in his crib, his face a pale blue as he struggled for breath, is not a memory he recalls but one he re-inhabits. It arrives without warning, a series of vivid, silent pictures: the frantic pattern of the wallpaper behind the crib, the paramedic’s face, the red glare of the ambulance lights washing over his wife’s tear-streaked cheeks. He finds he can never let the sequence play out to its conclusion in the hospital; his mind slams a door on it, pushing it away before he has to feel the full weight of his helplessness again.

Though his son made a full recovery, the world never returned to its proper shape for David. The constant, low-level hum of anxiety he now carries feels like a necessary shield. He has come to believe that the only reason his family is safe is because he is paying attention in a way he failed to before. At his analyst firm downtown, he can no longer sit with his back to the door. Before any meeting, he finds himself instinctively locating the exits, mapping a mental path out of the building. He tells himself it’s just being prepared, but the feeling of safety never arrives. The vigilance follows him home, becoming most acute at night. Sleep feels like a dereliction of duty. He lies awake for hours, straining to hear the sound of his son’s breathing through the monitor, certain that if he allows himself to drift off, he will miss a crucial sign and fail in his most fundamental role as a protector.

Over the past eight months, David’s world has shrunk. He used to enjoy taking his son to the park, but now the sight of other children, with their coughs and runny noses, triggers a surge of panic that is physical and overwhelming. He feels a desperate need to flee, to get his own son to safety. The weather has become a source of dread; a gray, rainy day like the one it all began on is enough to cast a pall of imminent danger over everything. He has stopped watching the news entirely, an almost impossible feat in his line of work, after a segment on a pediatric flu outbreak sent him into a tailspin, forcing him to leave the office and drive home just to check that his son was still breathing. This has had consequences. His manager has spoken to him about his erratic attendance and seeming lack of focus, things that were once his greatest professional strengths.

The most painful change, however, is internal. David feels like a stranger to himself. The calm, logical man who could analyze market volatility without flinching has been replaced by someone he doesn't recognize—a person governed by fear. He looks in the mirror and sees a fraud. The thought that circles endlessly is, "I should have seen it sooner. I should have protected him." This sense of failure has corroded his identity. He feels he is no longer the man his wife married, nor the father his son deserves. It was after he found himself unable to get out of the car for his nephew’s birthday party, paralyzed by the thought of all the children who would be inside, that his wife finally insisted he seek help. David agreed, not out of hope, but out of a profound sense of exhaustion. He is terrified that this new, broken version of himself is permanent, and what he wants more than anything is to simply feel like the man he used to be, before the rain came.
